2.title: Why is sleep testing so hard?
detailed: Let me start with a simple question: why is sleep testing so hard?
Look at the waiting room. If we suspect sleep-disordered breathing, we need objective data.
But getting that data is a real hassle.
Besides, putting on the sensors for the patient often takes more than 40 minutes, which makes patients anxious.
And patients have to sleep in a very unnatural setting.

3.title: How do today's tests compare?
detailed: Let's look at the options we have now. How do today's tests compare?
PSG covers all sleep diseases, but it needs 20 or more wires, and patients wait 1 or 2 months.
Home sleep testing uses 3 wires. An oximeter or an ECG patch can record for 7 to 14 days.
But they are all uncomfortable, and the patch can cause allergy.
So we need to move past wearable sensors, from Type I to Type IV, to monitoring with nothing to wear, night after night.

5.title: Radar principle diagram
detailed: Our answer is radar. Here is how it works.
The radar sends a signal from Tx, and picks up the reflection at Rx.
When the chest moves a little, the received signal changes, in its time of flight, or ToF, and its phase.
From the changes, we rebuild the breathing signal, with no wires.

7.title: Our three published studies: sleep lab, home, and heart
detailed: With this setup, our team has done three published studies: sleep lab, home, and heart.
How it works: a 24-GHz continuous-wave radar, plus deep neural decision trees.
In Study 1, in the sleep lab, we compared the radar side by side with PSG in 196 patients, and got a strong correlation, r = 0.91.
In Study 2, we tested 80 patients at home, for 147 nights, with no professional needed to set it up.
In Study 3, with 72 patients, when the radar picked up periodic breathing, it was linked to lower LVEF.

10.title: Sleep tests watch airflow. Radar watches the chest.
detailed: Why? Because sleep tests watch airflow, while radar watches the chest. They are two different signals.
In standard scoring, airflow stops, that's apnea, or gets shallow, that's hypopnea. We only see these events when we measure airflow.
Radar senses the chest rising and falling, not airflow.
And every patient is different: tall or short, thin or heavy, lying on the back or on the side.
So if we use a "normal" breathing size, and the usual apnea and hypopnea rules, on chest motion, the results can be far off.
There's one more problem. In an obstructive event, the upper airway is blocked. At first, chest motion drops a lot.
But as time goes on, the body starts to struggle to breathe.
A standard sleep test sees no airflow. But the radar sees the chest moving again.
So judging apnea by the size of chest motion has a big error. This is the biggest blind spot.
In our first year with the engineering team, we tried many methods. Nothing worked, and we almost gave up.
The way out was this: the radar has to spot a typical pattern of chest-motion changes.
That pattern ends with the recovery surge: when an event ends, the airway opens, and the person takes one big breath.
Let me show you a short video of what this looks like on the radar.

13.title: Study 1: How accurate is it in the hospital?
detailed: Beyond the correlation, Study 1 also asked: how accurate is it in the hospital?
Here, bRDI is the BestShape Respiratory Disturbance Index, from the radar.
The radar's bRDI and the AHI from PSG line up well, with a strong correlation.
For moderate-to-severe OSA, the accuracy was 90.3%.
And for severe OSA, the accuracy was 92.4%.
If we look at multi-class prediction, the average accuracy was 83.7%.

16.title: Study 2: How well does it work at home?
detailed: So how well does it work at home?
We got a strong Spearman correlation, ρ = 0.87, with p < 0.01. So bRDI_TIB tracks HSAT AHI closely, even with no one supervising.
For consistency, on average, the difference is −5.30 events/h.
And 93.88% of nights, that's 138 of 147, fall within the ±1.96 SD limits of agreement.

23.title: Decoding periodic breathing (PB)
detailed: So what exactly is periodic breathing?
Look at the top. Normal breathing is steady, with even waves.
Now look below. In periodic breathing, the breathing grows and fades: a phase of heavy breathing, then an apnea, again and again.
One heavy-breathing phase plus one apnea makes one cycle. The time it takes is the PB cycle length.
Periodic breathing is often seen in heart failure.
From the continuous radar signal, we can measure this cycle length, night after night.
And this number may give us a window into how well the heart pumps.

25.title: Two reasons breathing swings: OSA and heart failure
detailed: But why does breathing swing like this? There are two main reasons.
First, airway resistance, like in OSA. The body overreacts, then underreacts. Too much, then too little. So breathing becomes unstable.
Second, heart failure. The CO2 and oxygen signals are delayed, so breathing control is always one step behind.
That second reason is the one we care about today.

26.title: Why does a weaker heart change breathing during sleep?
detailed: Let's look closer at this loop. Why would a weaker heart change breathing during sleep?
Breathing is controlled by a feedback loop: the neural outflow, the plant gain, the circulation time, and the chemoreflex gain to CO2.
When the heart is weak, blood moves more slowly, so the circulation time gets longer. The loop reacts late, and breathing starts to swing.
So periodic breathing is associated with impaired cardiac function.
Just to be clear, our radar does not measure CO2. It only sees the breathing pattern.

27.title: Periodic-breathing features & cycle length
detailed: So how do we measure periodic breathing? We use features like the cycle length and the hyperpnea length.
Other teams have looked at this, too. The worse the heart, the longer the cycle.
One team looked back at CPAP data from the month before patients came to the emergency room with heart failure.
Measured by CPAP, the cycle length increased 11 times in acute heart failure, and 8 times in chronic heart failure, compared with 1 time in a normal heart.
And by LVEF, the cycle length goes from 49.1 seconds when LVEF is above 50, up to 85.7 seconds when LVEF is below 20.

And finally, we found associations between periodic breathing and cardiac impairment. So it may help us watch the heart, too.
